subsubtopic: FILLING OF CENSUS COMMISSIONER POSITIONS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. In view of the recent conformation at a provincial court case in Winnipeg by Mr. Harold Kenna, a program manager with Statistics Canada, that lists of Liberal party supporters to fill census commissioner positions for the 1976 census were sent out to Statistics Canada by the federal Liberal party, a practice which can be used for the purpose of gathering political information, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta):
That the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce instruct his departmental officials to abandon this obvious patronage policy which is undermining the political privacy of millions of Canadians, and adopt a policy whereby impartial lists, free of political affiliation, are given to Statistics Canada for the census commissioner.

subsubtopic: LOANS BY CORPORATION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent necessity to draw attention to recent loans made by the Export Development Corporation, one in the amount of $47 million and the other in the amount of $50 million, to the Beloit Company of Canada, Sorel, Quebec, a totally-owned subsidiary of the Beloit Company of Wisconsin, U.S.A., for the manufacture of newsprint machinery to be used by two American companies, namely, the Bato Company in Virginia and the Midtec Paper Corporation in Wisconsin. I, therefore,
ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
In view of the fact that the machinery thus produced will be used in the United States to produce paper in direct competition with Canadian paper producers, something which could result in serious loss of business and jobs in one of our major industries, the House condemns the action of the government in sacrificing the long-term health of a truly Canadian industry, namely, the pulp and paper industry, in favour of a short-term benefit to a Canadian machinery manufacturer which is wholly-owned by American interests; and, finally, that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce explain to the House why such steps were taken by ministerial order against the recommendations of senior officials of the Export Development Corporation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to seek the unanimous consent of the House on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that Mr. Bill Watkins, a constituent of mine, has been charged under the Statistics Act with failing to complete a census form, that the section of the form which Mr. Watkins refused to complete did not provide for the accurate listing of the mother tongue of his children, which was neither English nor French but was both, since the children are fluently bilingual, that Mr. Watkins had pointed out this failing in the census form to the chief statistician in 1971 and had been informed that the census form would be changed, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That this House urge the government to charge the responsible minister with an infringement of section 8(1) of the Statistics Act for discrimination against bilingual Canadians and, further, that this House urge the government to introduce a special bill to cover the legal expenses of Mr. Watkins incurred for contesting this charge brought against him by this government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General: it relates to the ongoing policies of the government regarding the confidentiality of income tax returns. Does it remain the government's policy to permit law enforcement officers access to confidential income tax returns in files of private citizens who are reasonably suspected of being involved in organized crime?

subtopic: ACCESS OF FORCE TO INCOME TAX RETURNS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is very much aware of the terms of the agreement entered into between the Department of National Revenue and the Solicitor General. The terms are self-explanatory. Both the Department of National Revenue and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police comply very specifically with the terms of that agreement.

subtopic: ACCESS OF FORCE TO INCOME TAX RETURNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General is aware that access is only permitted on the basis of a citizen being suspected of being involved in organized crime, the official definition of which is "two or more persons concerting together on a continuing basis to participate in illegal activities either directly or indirectly for gain." It has been pointed out in the McDonald commission that that could include a husband and wife conspiring together to cheat on an unemployment insurance claim.
In the area of access by law enforcement officers to confidential income tax files of those suspected of being involved in organized crime, is this rather broad definition used, or is a more restricted, pertinent definition of organized crime used to permit that access? If so, what is that more restricted definition?

subtopic: ACCESS OF FORCE TO INCOME TAX RETURNS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member fully knows if he has read the proceedings before the McDonald inquiry, the definition was one suggested by counsel through a leading question. I can assure the hon. member that the definition relating to a husband and wife attempting to conspire to defraud the unemployment insurance system is not one which is of any interest to the RCMP.

subtopic: ACCESS OF FORCE TO INCOME TAX RETURNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Solicitor General knows full well, that definition has been accepted by the minister and by
[Mr. Nystrom.l
the commissioner of the RCMP, in committee, as being the only official definition of organized crime. Is access being granted to confidential income tax returns on the basis of that definition? If not, on the basis of what definition is such access being given?

subtopic: ACCESS OF FORCE TO INCOME TAX RETURNS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman knows that the purpose of the agreement was to permit co-operation between National Revenue and the RCMP in order to prosecute offences under the Income Tax Act. In terms of non-compliance with the Income Tax Act, there has, indeed, been information made available by the RCMP to National Revenue that permitted these prosecutions. Surely the hon. gentleman knows that the full purpose was to deal with individuals who are known to, or who are suspected of engaging in activities that come within the definition of organized crime as the hon. gentleman understands that definition.

speechtext:

I ask the minister whether, in getting out of direct financing the federal government has obtained specific commitments from the banks and other lending institutions that they will fill this financing gap at low interest rates.
I ask this question in light of the failure of the former minister, the Minister of National Defence, who promised us
June 7, 1978

in 1975 that we would get $1 billion in financing for housing from the banks, but it turned out that we got only $300 million.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
maintopic: MORTGAGE PAYMENTS UNDER CO-OPERATIVE HOUSING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in our negotiations with the lending institutions, I could say that while they have some reservations and a prudent and cautious approach to the proposal of the graduated payment mortgage, on the other hand their responses to our initiative on the low income housing proposal were very positive. The lenders responded positively to the federal initiative in this area and indicated a willingness to invest in social housing programs in support of provincial, municipal or private non-profit or co-operative associations.
We have received this assurance from the lending institutions, and therefore we believe that the provinces or the private non-profit or co-operative groups could get the money from the banks. We have indicated that, at any rate, the federal government could be there as a banker of last resort.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right hon. Prime Minister. Given the fact that the Premier of Ontario has abdicated his responsibilities with respect to the linguistic situation, given the urgency there is to stop the galloping assimilation of the French-speaking minorities living in provinces with an English-speaking majority and, finally, in order to secure a federal leadership which will assure the existence of a united Canada which will respect the rights of all Canadians, can the right hon. Prime Minister tell the House whether he intends to table very soon the constitutional proposals he promised in the Speech from the Throne in order to enshrine in the Canadian Constitution, before it is too late, the fundamental rights in the field of linguistic equality and justice which will allow all Canadians to achieve their legitimate aspirations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 will remind the hon. member of what he surely already knows, and I mean that since 1969 at the least, the federal government has been making proposals to the provinces aimed at enshrining into the Constitution an unfailing protection for the rights of the minorities, whether they are the French-speaking minorities in the rest of the country or the English-speaking minority in Quebec. Those proposals are to be reiterated and restated in the proposals the government will table before this House within a few weeks.
Oral Questions

AUTOMOTIVE PLANTS IN ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Can the minister advise the House of the proposals he and his officials have made to General Motors, Ford and others regarding the establishment of a new automobile assembly plant and a parts plant in Ontario and Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE PLANTS IN ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have been over this one several times in the House. I have said repeatedly that when I have an announcement to make, I will be only too glad to make it. To date I have no announcement to make.

subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE PLANTS IN ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister confirm that this package of more than $150 million is broken down into roughly $50 million each for Ford and General Motors? speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE PLANTS IN ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:

June 7, 1978
Oral Questions
1980, can the minister indicate what priority she is giving to Bill C-55 and her proposal for the debating schedule?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

subtopic: USE OF CANADIAN RAIL CARS BY U.S.
USE OF CANADIAN RAIL CARS BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Last week, the president of the Canadian Transport Commission indicated there were some 23,000 CN railway cars located in the United States and said this was some 13,000 more than would be considered normal. He further indicated that the U.S. railways are using these rail cars for the movement of goods in the United States and are getting their use at no charge.
Has the minister looked into this matter, or will he look into it? Would this type of subject come under the consideration of the new special investigating committee announced last week by the hon. member for Assiniboia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: USE OF CANADIAN RAIL CARS BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this committee would not normally consider the expediting of grain movement. Grain cars as such are rarely involved in this problem with United States traffic, since they are rarely moved into the United States for any great distance.

There is a higher than normal number of cars in the United States. A number of factors contribute to this, including a combination of heavy traffic into the United States, some difficult weather conditions during the winter and, without doubt, some weaknesses in the United States rail system which cause an increasing number of slow orders to be issued across the rail system, thereby slowing down the return of the cars.
There is a penalty or payment in respect of many of these cars when they are used against the rules; indeed, when they are used in any case. My information is that this penalty was doubled recently so that there would be more inducement for the cars to be brought home. We are still not satisfied with the situation and are paying close attention to it to see whether other steps can be taken to ensure the return of cars, particularly in the case of potash and lumber, more quickly than at present.

subtopic: USE OF CANADIAN RAIL CARS BY U.S.
speechtext:
The minister indicated that none of these cars would be used for the movement of grain. That point of view is different from that of the president of the Canadian Transport Commission.
I have a related question, Mr. Speaker. Since many points in western Canada will not be able to take advantage of the current delivery quotas which will terminate on June 9, for example, Kyle, Saskatchewan, where some 300,000 bushels are waiting to be shipped, with trucks lined up, is consideration being given to extending the termination date for quotas so that the grain can be moved to port position?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: USE OF CANADIAN RAIL CARS BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated in my earlier answer that grain cars as such are not involved in movements to the United States. Obviously, there are occasions when potash cars which are no longer needed for carrying potash could be helpful. I do not deny that there may be some slight implication for grain movement in relation to cars.
As far as quotas are concerned, I can tell the hon. member that the Wheat Board, as ever, is watchful of the situation of whether farmers are able to deliver on quota. It has already announced its extension of the June 9 quota date to June 30.

maintopic: STUDY OF WESTERN CANADA GRAIN HANDLING
STUDY OF WESTERN CANADA GRAIN HANDLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Transport. On June 3, the government made what turned out to be a form of press statement in Saskatchewan. The general thrust of it is that they are going to initiate one more study with regard to grain transportation in western Canada.
Will the minister inform the House who the government will appoint for that study, the length of time it will take, and will he outline some of the general guidelines that the person who will be appointed to carry out the study, for whatever reason it is being done, will operate under?
June 7, 1978

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
maintopic: STUDY OF WESTERN CANADA GRAIN HANDLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the appointment has not yet been made. The study is being undertaken because we are not certain we have done everything that can be done; that is to say, we collectively, the railways, the elevator companies, the Wheat Board and all the rest, in order to get the maximum out of the equipment we have. We have done a great deal. We have the bloc shipping system, co-ordinators at the terminals, some improvements in the way cars are handled by the railways, and I could go on to many more things.
There are some very difficult constrictions in the system, such as union relationships at the terminal and the relationship among the elevator operators and their managers with regard to hours of work. There are some in the way the railways handle their cars and give them priority. It is our intention to again study these fundamental problems, with the optimistic view that we will not stop at the first objection from one or another of the parties involved that it is difficult to accomplish a particular end. We will go beyond that and look with imagination at how that goal can be accomplished so that we can get perhaps 40 per cent more use out of all the hopper cars that we are acquiring.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER NAVAL VESSELS REPAIR PROGRAM WILL BE ACCELERATED
INQUIRY WHETHER NAVAL VESSELS REPAIR PROGRAM WILL BE ACCELERATED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. I would like to know whether his department has secured the necessary funds, that is $2 million, following tenders which have been received for the building of the Protector for which the Davie Shipbuilding had made the lowest bid at $9 million.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER NAVAL VESSELS REPAIR PROGRAM WILL BE ACCELERATED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are looking at this matter very carefully. We hope to be able to find the funds to make this work possible in the St. Lawrence shipyards as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. It relates to the progress or, perhaps more accurately, the lack of progress with regard to the plant breeders' rights legislation. The plant breeders
Oral Questions
require this legislation: they have been asking for it for months and the government has promised it for months. I simply ask the minister when we can expect to see the legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much whether the legislation will be brought in before the end of this month. It depends on how long the House sits. If it is not brought in at this time, it will be given a priority position in the early fall.

I am disappointed by the minister's response and I am certain the plant breeders will share my view. Can we get an assurance from the minister that this legislation will not be like the Canadian meat import law and the stabilization payment to beef producers-promised and never delivered? These kinds of promises we can do without.
Mr. Speaker, our plant breeders have been without this kind of legislation since plant breeding began in Canada. If they do get it, it will be something they have never had before.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Agriculture. speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can understand why the hon. member is concerned about the one in this area. I signed a press release on this and outlined that the regulations would be announced very shortly for people such as the hon. member is talking about who want to take advantage of the program. People in the feed deficient areas of eastern Ontario, western Quebec and eastern Canada, will be able to take advantage of this program. We hope to have the regulations by the end of this week or the first part of next week so they will know how to apply.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the minister of industry, trade and tourism or the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Can he report any progress as far as the Halifax shipyard is concerned? He must have been made aware by his confreres in the province of Nova Scotia that many of the shipyard workers are running out of unemployment insurance. Will there be a buyer for the shipyard? If not, why does the government not take it over and run it?

June 7, 1978
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are carrying on conversations with the Nova Scotia government and the owners of the Halifax shipyard in the hope that if they no longer want to run it, between the three of us we can find someone who will take it over and continue the business of repairing ships at Halifax.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON UNDERSEA ENERGY RESOURCES
CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON UNDERSEA ENERGY RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. According to published reports today, the minister's Canadian negotiators on the undersea boundary dispute question have proposed a shared 50-50 access to oil and gas production in disputed territories with the United States. My question to the minister is, is this true?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON UNDERSEA ENERGY RESOURCES
speechtext: Without being the least offensive, Mr. Speaker, 1 do not think I ought to tell the hon. member. It is obviously part of a negotiating posture. It is a story in the newspapers. However, I would not want to confirm or deny it in precisely the language the hon. member has put to me. If he can rephrase the question in some way, I will be glad to be as forthcoming as I can.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON UNDERSEA ENERGY RESOURCES
speechtext: Regarding any giveaway of undersea mineral rights on the continental Canadian shelf, regarding which many Canadian provinces feel they have a very just claim- and that view is shared by many in the country and in this House-may I ask the minister if any of the provinces concerned were involved in the discussions ahead of time, or will they be before any such offer is made to the United States?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON UNDERSEA ENERGY RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can answer that question clearly. We have had discussions with the provinces and we are continuing to discuss the matter with them. I am speaking from memory, but I do not think there has been any firm position taken by either side. A number of possibilities are being explored. As I understand it, even if a clearcut line is delineated there is a necessity for some agreement on each side of the line because deposits, particularly our deposits, may be located under the seabed on each side of that dividing line. So there are some complications involved. But the provinces are being consulted and we shall take their representations very much into consideration in reaching any final decision.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON UNDERSEA ENERGY RESOURCES
speechtext: A final question. Does the minister not think it possible that we could at least discuss this subject in the House, with the minister leading the way, and consider some of the legal questions involving jurisdiction, instead of some of us having to pick these things up in the newspapers? Could we not discuss these things in the House first?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADA-U.S. NEGOTIATIONS ON UNDERSEA ENERGY RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not know what mechanism might be adopted. There are two considerations involved. One is the restriction imposed during the question period. The other is this: I do not know whether members opposite would genuinely wish to get into a discussion in terms of indicating what the posture is while the negotiations are under way. However, in committee or anywhere else where it could be done without causing problems to our negotiators, we would have no objection to the subject being dealt with. We have asked the provinces for their views, and there is no reason why we should not let members in on our position.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 gave you the usual notice of my intention to raise a question of privilege on a matter I brought to your attention yesterday evening. It relates to the performance of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: A great performance!

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: It is interesting to note the kind of action on the part of this minister that government supporters are applauding. I raise this matter because I feel it is one which should receive serious attention by Your Honour and by members of the House. We have, unfortunately, become used to intemperate and petty outbursts from the government side.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
We regret that the minister is incapable of making his point in debate without indulging in personal reflections. Members on both sides of the House occasionally infringe the rules in their warmth of expression and are usually quick to withdraw any remarks of theirs which the Speaker has described as unparliamentary. I hope the minister will take this opportunity to improve his record in this regard.
Yesterday evening, the minister stated:
But instead of grappling with it, the Conservatives go into Anglophone Canada and feed it with their lies and deceptions and their urgings to hate.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be hard to imagine language which more grossly offends against the standard usually enforced in this House. It was suggested yesterday that the minister saved himself by referring to the Conservative party generally. I agree that vague references have often been passed over. However, I suggest that in this case the violence of the language, and the fact that western members appear to be singled out by a subsequent statement of the minister, removes that defence.
June 7, 1978

For similar language, Mr. Speaker, a member of this party was ejected from the House two weeks ago. The words "lie" and "liar" have always been withdrawn after being used in this House. I also suggest that the words "urgings to hatred" offend the spirit of Beauchesne 155, in that they accuse a member of base and offensive motives.
It would not be very gracious of the minister to fall back on the defence that he did not single out a particular member, but accused all of them. It seems to me that a minister of the Crown should be fully supportive of the dignity of the House, and realize that we are here to debate policies and not debase the personal reputation of fellow members.
In the interest of preventing the kind of breakdown in the House that I know Your Honour would like to avoid, I hope the minister will take this opportunity to withdraw the remarks and allegations he made yesterday.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think it is clear that the language I used does not fall within the definition of what is considered unparliamentary. I agree that it is strong language; statements about "lies" and "deception" do, indeed, constitute strong language. Nevertheless, the fact of the matter is that I have frequently seen this used as a tactic, particularly in western Canada, and what I was addressing last night was the serious consequence for this country of that tactic being used in a way which permits, preaches and evokes dislike for either a region of the country or of a particular linguistic group. I have seen this time and time again.
I would be delighted to have a committee of the House look into the question of how these things are done and how hatred and separation are spread. 1 recall one instance particularly in the home town of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) which I share with him. It was very clear from the Conservative advertising that they were suggesting a Quebec plot-it would be funny if it were not so sad. They said the picture of the prairies had been removed from the dollar bill and replaced by a picture of the Parliament Buildings taken from the Hull side.
Going on from there, you have a greater combination of suspicion and lies. The example I used last night had to do with the way in which Conservatives across the country assert that the government is favouring the province of Quebec in DREE programs, winter works programs and the like. The fact is that Quebec may indeed benefit more than Ontario, Alberta or some other province, but in all cases it derives less benefit than the Atlantic provinces because the principle is to try to help those areas which most need help.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: At the very time we are making our case against the separatists in Quebec, pointing out that the province does receive a good deal from the federal treasury given the economic circumstances of the province, we find these neo-separatists from other parts of the country spreading dislike-

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Privilege-Mr. Hnatyshyn

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
Order, please. There is a natural temptation for hon. members to get into the merits of the question when words such as "lies" and "deception" have been used, and to go behind such phrases to demonstrate a certain position or support a certain argument. Nevertheless, I think we should avoid going into the merits and confine ourselves to the procedural question.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has indicated that the description he was using was not applied to members of the House of Commons but to Conservatives generally.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
Order. On a straight reading of the language objected to, I would be prepared to accept that possibility. However, I go back to the beginning of his remarks, to the paragraph in the middle of the second column of Hansard at page 6126. In cases where there is any possibility that unparliamentary expressions have been directed against members of the House, I think we have to take action quickly.
The minister says now that he did not intend to direct this comment against members of the House of Commons and, if that is so, I will ask him to make that perfectly clear because of the following language the minister has used. I will read it without including interjections:
What we have in this House... is a Conservative opposition which does not care to consider the impact on this country's unity and which does not care indeed if its actions, time and time again, drive wedges between people in this country... The hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) shrieks ... but let me tell him about colleagues of his having urged in this House on the one hand that the Minister of Finance immediately pay the money to the government of Quebec, when they would have gone across certain areas of this country saying to the people in the rest of Canada-in Saskatchewan where I live and in neighbouring provinces-
And so forth. In light of that language, if the Minister of Transport was endeavouring to make an accusation only a few lines later in respect to Conservatives outside the House and not members in the House, that certainly is not the context which is described by the language which I have just referred to; and if the Minister of Transport says today that he was talking about Conservative organizers and so forth, he is excused. However, on the basis of this language I would have to have him state here in this House that that language somehow did not refer to members of the House of Commons, and that if he did refer to members of the House of Commons he now withdraws that remark in respect to members of the House.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure I understand your adjudication.

subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
I would like to make it perfectly clear that in the later reference to lies and deceptions I was referring to a

June 7, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Hnatyshyn
general Conservative tactic and conduct and certainly not specifically to any members of parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Cheap.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: In the earlier one I did indeed, I think, describe exactly what I thought they did in the way of a tactic, in terms of talking one way in this House and talking another way outside the House. That did apply to members. But I am presuming that Your Honour does not indicate that that earlier reference is the unparliamentary one, so I do separate those two very completely.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: What I am saying is that the combination of the two references, so closely related, leads to a very clear suspicion, which the minister says is not the case. We accept the word of members in this House, but it leads to the clear impression that the two are tied together. He separates them in his mind, and I accept that; however, I would want the minister to make clear today the intent of the language he used, "lies and deceptions". I think we always have to be very careful. When we enter into that kind of language, we have to be absolutely clear that it is not in reference to members of the House of Commons, and I would want the minister now to make it absolutely clear that he was not making that reference in relation to members of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is what I meant to do in my previous intervention. I do not so intend.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. HNATYSHYN-REMARKS OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT IN DEBATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the national Leader of the Progressive Conservative party and as a member of this House, I am responsible in quite general terms for the strategy of my party. It is that very strategy which was attacked by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) last night in the House of Commons.

I am quite prepared to accept the ruling which Your Honour has made and the retraction you have extracted from the Minister of Transport. I will accept that on the very narrow procedural grounds which are the grounds to which Your Honour, by necessity, is confined.
What is of greater concern to me here, as I am sure it is to all hon. members of the House of Commons, is that we know that in this House we set a standard which is followed elsewhere in the country and which forms attitudes toward the goodwill which exists among peoples and regions in this country and also toward the very delicate and difficult question of national unity in this country. I think that whatever the technical ruling Your Honour has made in relation to this intemperate, unfortunate statement by the Minister of Transport, it is very clear that when a senior minister of the Crown of Canada can stand up in the House of Commons and make that kind of allegation, designed in its way to create apprehensions about the Progressive Conservative party and also designed to undermine and to sow discord in the country and

to create suspicions where no suspicions should exist, then, sir,
I think we have a rather different circumstance.
I quite accept that the circumstance which has arisen now as a result of the unfortunate, irresponsible and childish remarks of the Minister of Transport is one which cannot be dealt with in any further procedural way by Your Honour. But we have in the House with us now-and I appreciate his staying at my request-the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the leader of the party of the minister who has made this allegation against the Progressive Conservative party as a whole in the country and who has made these statements which clearly can lead to a very serious hostility in the country.
The Prime Minister has heard these remarks stated. He was not here yesterday. I recall that in 1968 when the Prime Minister was campaigning in his first election as leader of his party he had the courage and the courtesy, when faced with an advertisement placed in the name of the then Liberal candidate in Calgary South which made similar unfounded allegations against the Progressive Conservative party, to dissociate himself as leader of his party from those irresponsible remarks, and I hope that the Prime Minister of Canada will use this opportunity here, not to hide himself behind the narrow grounds which have provided some protection under the rules to the Minister of Transport, but instead to accept his larger responsibility to national unity and stand in his place and dissociate himself from the statements which have been made by the Minister of Transport.

In so far as the comment was not made about members of the House of Commons, it is a comment which can be made by the Minister of Transport.
Debate on the bill will carry on today. There will be a few hours of debate later on this afternoon, and if there are to be further replies, they can be made in that debate.
In so far as there was an unparliamentary use of language, that has been corrected procedurally. But there are ways of answering the allegations-or repeating them, in fact-if in fact they are parliamentary allegations; and in so far as they do not apply to members of this House, no procedural objections can arise.
I see that the Minister of Transport wants to answer the Leader of the Opposition. I think it is only fair that he make a response and then, from a procedural point of view, the matter ought to be closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

Mr. Speaker, I need not take a great amount of time to respond, but I think the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) did in fact impute motives to me in terms of trying to create some unfortunate and disastrous results in the country by my comments.

I would just like to assure him that my motives are very much based on the hope that he may take his responsibilities and correct the actions which go on in the Conservative party so that there will not be seized the advantage of prejudices which do exist. If the Leader of the Opposition does not know how extensive they are, I ask him to accept the offer I also extended to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), and that is to let me take him to certain areas in the west and let him hear how deeply these divisions are sown. I have the hope that his party, as one of the traditional and ancient parties in this country, will adopt a standard designed to unite the country and not divide it and feed on prejudice.

speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member misunderstands, and I will say it one more time. Procedurally, members of the House of Commons are restricted in making allegations in various forms of unparliamentary language against members of the House of Commons. They are not under the same constraints in respect of other groups of people. Therefore, if
Privilege-Mr. Hnatyshyn
any member of the House feels himself aggrieved as part of a larger group, there are several recourses for him. If it is a political aspersion, it can be defended in a political circle; if it is a debating point, it can be carried on in the debate this afternoon. But on procedural grounds, the minister has made an allegation which, in my opinion, indicated it may be directed at members of the House of Commons, and in so far as it was, it was unparliamentary. Therefore, I insisted that it be withdrawn in respect of members of the House of Commons.
I think hon. members should understand that the precedents indicate quite clearly that a general aspersion against a group of people, whether it happens to include members of the House of Commons or not, is not to be included in those parliamentary categories. Therefore, whether a member of the House of Commons incidentally, as part of a larger group, feels himself aggrieved by the aspersion is beside the point.
In any case, I have ruled on the matter procedurally and the minister has indicated his withdrawal of any unparliamentary remarks in the sense that they might have been directed at members of the opposition here, and that closes the matter procedurally.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on an entirely different question of privilege. Earlier in the question period, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), either deliberately or inadvertently-and I am assuming the latter until he clarifies the record-told the House that under the changes announced in the housing program those who are going to get a subsidy for mortgages in the co-op housing section would get a mortgage of 1 per cent for 35 years. The clear, commonsense interpretation of that answer is that anyone who is in a co-op housing project would get that 1 per cent mortgage for 35 years.
As the minister surely knows, the reality is that such is not the case. According to a document which was circulated by his own department in the month of May, the reality is that someone in a co-op housing project might get a subsidy down to the 1 per cent level and might get it extended year after year for up to 35 years. Because of other changes made in the regulations by his department, it is most unlikely that anything approaching a significant number of people going to that co-op project, would be eligible for a 1 per cent mortgage and subsidy, on the assumption that a significant number in that project were eligible for a 1 per cent mortgage subsidy.
That is a very important point because the minister, in his remarks today, left the impression that there is a fundamental change in policy which will be to the advantage of the co-ops rather than, as many of them see it, to their disadvantage.
I should like him to clarify the record on that point and make it clear that it is just possible that a few people might get a subsidy down to the 1 per cent level. In that context, would he clarify the other concern which is directly related?

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order in respect of questions on the order paper, and I would beg your indulgence for a couple of moments, sir.
On January 25 I placed a question on the order paper, No. 1,216, which reads as follows:
For each department, what was the total expenditure on air travel during the last year for which figures are available and, in each case, how much was for (a) domestic (b) overseas flights?
A return was tabled last Friday, and I would have been reluctantly prepared to accept the advice of the President of Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) when his return was tabled as follows:
The information on all air travel booked directly by each department i.e. last minute reservations, etc., is not readily available. To provide an accurate reply would entail a lengthy and costly examination of thousands of travel claims for every department, which cost in manpower and time would be exorbitant or prohibitive.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I would have been reluctantly prepared to accept that, but we have received further answers in respect of that same question. We find that the Department of National Defence did give a reply to the effect that, because of the complexity of the question, they could not answer it. I would have been happy with that as well.
However, we have an answer in respect of the Department of External Affairs, and it was at this point that I began to feel that the House was being misled by the minister or the office
Point of Order-Mr. Alexander
of the President of Privy Council, or that they were at least being less than honest with members of parliament. This department did answer the question. They were able to come up with the figure of some $4 million.
That is not the end of it, sir. We then received another return, and this is most important because sometimes I find that the office of the President of Privy Council is less than co-operative. I do not suggest officials intentionally attempt to mislead the House, but in this case at least I think they were less than honest. The return from the Department of Supply and Services is as follows:
Insofar as the Department of Supply and Services is concerned:
The total expenditure on air travel booked through the Central Travel Service of the Department of Supply and Services was $30,539,494.00 in 1976-77, the last year for which complete figures are available.
Information is not accessible on the division between domestic and overseas flights.
My point of order arises from the return tabled by the President of the Privy Council through the parliamentary secretary which, in effect, states that the question is too complex, would cost too much money to answer, would call for the expenditure of a tremendous amount of manpower, and accordingly will not be answered department by department. We then find a department answering the same question, namely the Department of Supply and Services, which refers to expenditures in terms of air travel for 67 agencies, including the departments.
I suggest there are too many of these stock type of answers. With all due respect, the parliamentary secretary has egg on his face. I hope in the future when questions are replied to there will be some co-ordination. The replies to question 1,216 would indicate there is something lacking in respect of co-ordination of answers given to questions on the order paper.

Mr. Speaker, we guarantee one thing: the most serious and complete research possible in order to give answers that are as complete and as accurate as possible. Unfortunately, we cannot give the hon. member a guarantee that he will be satisfied, on the political level, with the replies he receives. We are not here in this House to serve the political ends of the hon. member; we are here, at the taxpayers' expense, to try to give him the most complete answers possible.
As was explained in the reply in most of the departments concerned we could not obtain the requested details; that is why, because of the costs and the time factor involved, the hon. member did not get the answer he had requested. For-tunatly, in some cases, he did get a global amount but no breakdown, precisely for the reasons explained in the reply we gave him. In short, Mr. Speaker, once again, the employees of the Privy Council office always do their best to give hon. members on both sides of the House the most responsible,

June 7, 1978
Motions for Papers
honest, accurate and complete answers possible. That has been our attitude in this session when up to now we have already replied to 73 per cent of all questions on the order paper. So I would ask the hon. member to be more understanding and much more courteous, and not to think when we answer questions that we are trying to mislead the House. Such is definitely not our motivation. Once again, we are not here to look after the political yearnings of the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the parliamentary secretary question No. 1,295 which I placed on the order paper on February 7. It is a simple question asked of the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) regarding a program called "Open House Canada". I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary could look into the matter and find out why it is taking so long to getting around to answering it.

Mr. Speaker,
I also have a complaint in respect of delays in answering order paper questions. Last year on December 7 I placed question No. 895 on the other paper as follows:
Are Members of Parliament entitled to use DOT Telex "Comcen" facilities for the purpose of sending political messages to their constituency and, if so, how many members used such facilities in 1976-77-
That was six months ago. Last fall 1 presented evidence at a committee meeting that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) was being allowed to use DOT telex facilities to send out political-and I have to refer to it as "garbage". We are entitled to an answer as to how many Liberal members are allowed to use this DOT telex network to send out political messages. This is information that could have been provided within a week. Here we are six months later without an answer.
I realize this is a very embarrassing question to the government but, nevertheless, I am entitled to an answer. Six months is a ridiculous length of time to provide an answer to a question like that. I would like the parliamentary secretary to look into the matter and give some indication as to when 1 can expect to receive an answer.
